standing_rules: A skip is not a success; an empty state is not a clean one; measured zero must look different from never ran.
Never fail-soft a create call; preserve the error envelope.
'Set in the environment' and 'works' are different claims — run check:secrets before blaming code.
Run the SQL with the merge, never after.
An unpriced model id fails loud, never $0.
Trust source, git log, and the tracker over any prose claiming completeness; close items with file:line in the same commit.
Ledger what is unproven — today: the publish->lift loop, and each UI surface until its soak passes.
Closing a task is an act on a verifier's word, never the implementer's. The agent that wrote the code never closes it.
A change to the orchestration tooling is itself ledger work. The machine is not exempt from the discipline it enforces.
Trace a call site to an HTTP route or a cron entry before describing it as live. A correct file:line proves a line exists, not that anything reaches it.

Close an item only when, in the same commit, its box is ticked, the commit body cites the file:line where the change lives, and the acceptance criterion was exercised — run, not read and not reasoned about. If it could not be exercised here, the item is blocked with the reason, never closed.

SURVEY FIRST: the accept's two clauses were already true and already tested — scanRoute.route.test.mjs proves 429 + x-ratelimit-limit 5 + remaining 0 on the 6th request and that the threshold follows SCAN_RATE_LIMIT, over the real POST handler. What was NOT true is that 'one IP' meant an IP. clientBucketKey read x-real-ip first, unconditionally, and x-real-ip is a request header. REPRODUCED against the real module + the real in-memory counter at SCAN_RATE_LIMIT=5: 25 requests with a rotating x-real-ip were allowed 25/25; 25 with a rotating x-forwarded-for were allowed 25/25; and 25 where x-vercel-forwarded-for named ONE client the whole time but x-real-ip rotated were also allowed 25/25. The counter was never wrong, the identity was. FIX (rateLimit.js:73 resolveClientIp): trust ordering, not header ordering. x-vercel-forwarded-for is used first and marked trusted ONLY when VERCEL/VERCEL_URL is set (Vercel strips inbound x-vercel-*; off Vercel that header is as forgeable as any other and is now ignored rather than promoted). SCAN_RATE_LIMIT_IP_HEADER lets a non-Vercel operator declare the header their proxy OVERWRITES. x-real-ip / leftmost x-forwarded-for remain as fallbacks but are reported trusted:false and warn once per process that the limit is bypassable by rotating that header — rule 1: a limit that quietly stops limiting must say so. After the fix all four spoof scenarios give 5 allowed / 20 refused. EXERCISED BY RUNNING, not reading: 33 tests across rateLimit.test.mjs (22, +7), scanRoute.route.test.mjs (7, untouched, still green) and the new scanRateLimitSpoof.route.test.mjs (4) — the last drives the REAL POST /api/scan handler with a trusted address plus two forged ones and asserts which counter moved (trusted 5->6, both forgeries still 5). That seed was added after the first negative-control run returned 201 and started an in-memory scan; no credentials are loaded under node --test so nothing was billed, but the hazard is now closed. Migration 007 adds a unique partial index on lower(btrim(brand)) over the running statuses. The predicate cannot include heartbeat freshness (partial-index predicates must be IMMUTABLE), so createScanJob resolves the violation: a live holder is a typed DuplicateScanError -> 409, a crashed holder is failed and the insert retried once, so a brand is never locked forever. isDuplicateScanViolation is deliberately narrow — a connection error or a different constraint is NOT reported as 'already scanning'. A drift guard fails if db.js SCAN_JOB_RUNNING and the index predicate disagree. Exercised against a REAL PostgreSQL 16 cluster started locally, not just unit-tested.

verification.note: Both clauses exercised for real. Started a local PostgreSQL 16 cluster, applied 001+005+007: 007 applies cleanly and is idempotent on re-run (NOTICE ... skipping, no error). Then two GENUINELY CONCURRENT psql sessions inserted a running scan_jobs row for the same brand with different casing ('Italica' vs 'ITALICA'): session 2 blocked on the index and then failed with 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint scan_jobs_one_running_per_brand', exactly one row survived. Rejection is therefore by the database, not application logic. Also confirmed complete/failed jobs do not block a new scan, and that failing a stale holder lets the retry insert succeed. 8 unit tests; the SCAN_JOB_RUNNING drift guard proven by removing a status from the predicate and watching it fail. Suite 667/667.

tasks.title: The Bright Data zone cache never invalidates
tasks.detail: resolveBrightDataSerpZone caches the auto-discovered zone in a module-level cachedZoneName with no TTL and no invalidation path. In a request-scoped Vercel function that is harmless, because the module reloads. In the long-lived worker container built by R1.2.1 it is not: a zone that is suspended, deleted or exhausted mid-run keeps being used until someone restarts the process, and every probe then fails for a reason the fleet cannot see. Found while testing R0.1.10, where a no-active-zone fixture silently returned the previous test cached value instead of throwing — the cache is invisible until it misleads you.
tasks.accept: The resolved zone is re-checked at least once per fleet poll cycle, or the cache carries a TTL; a zone that stops being active surfaces as a typed configuration error rather than as N failed probes.

POLICY: three levers, combined, not one chosen. (1) TTL — cachedZone is now {name, at} (brightdata.js:81) and resolve serves it only while fresh (:145); default 5 minutes (:72), overridable via BRIGHTDATA_ZONE_TTL_MS, 0 = never cache. A malformed TTL throws instead of falling back to the default (:91) — a silent fallback would tell an operator who wrote '30s' that they had a 30s re-check while a dead zone lived on for five minutes. (2) invalidateBrightDataZoneCache() (:116) is exported for the R1.2 fleet to force a re-check per poll cycle; it returns the dropped name, or null when nothing was cached, so 'cleared' and 'was already empty' are different events. (3) Probe-time rejection: zoneRejectionDetail (:291) reads Bright Data's zone refusals out of the HTTP body (:398) and the 200 envelope (:445), zoneRejectedError (:313) drops the cache and returns a typed BrightDataZoneError, and the retry loop refuses to retry one (:478). Recovery is therefore ONE failed probe, not one TTL; the TTL is the backstop for the case Bright Data never tells us about. Per-probe re-listing was rejected on cost: get_all_zones is a real call and that would be ~30 extra per scan. WHY NOT PER-PROBE, WHY BOTH CONSUMERS ARE SERVED: web requests (aioPipeline/enginePipeline) never get to call an invalidator, so they need the clock; a 5-minute TTL is longer than a typical invocation, so their cost profile is unchanged at one lookup per process. The fleet gets the clock AND the explicit invalidator. A re-check that could not be COMPLETED (get_all_zones itself failing) throws lookup_failed and does NOT refresh the timestamp — a grace window serving the stale name through an outage was considered and rejected as exactly the fail-soft this task removes. TYPED, NOT SILENT: BrightDataZoneError carries reason no_active_zone|zone_rejected|lookup_failed|bad_ttl_config, and a re-check that changes nothing logs 'still active' so 'the TTL fired and all is well' cannot be confused with 'the TTL never fired'. R0.1.10 IS NOT REGRESSED: a rejected probe is still an ERROR row and still counted — brightdataZone.test.mjs:334 keeps errored_queries 1 / error_rate_pct 100 and gains an assertion that a PINNED bad zone says it cannot self-heal. tasks.detail: R1.2.2's two six-worker cases in src/lib/probeTasksRace.test.mjs carry NO atomicity teeth: its verifier ran them against a claim function with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED stripped and both still passed. VERIFIED, third round. All ten citations resolve to the mechanism they name, checked in the MAIN tree where the ledger points: :28 ledger DDL, :192 BEGIN, :200 the checksum comment, :215 the INSERT, :222 COMMIT in the same try, :250 the INCOMPLETE condition AND :255 its exit, plus migrationsRunner.test.mjs:262/:277 and migrationsLedger.test.mjs:98. THE STREAM SEPARATION IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT DECORATIVE, and the verifier proved it independently: console.error in the same slot lands at the end of a concatenated buffer and would read as "after" the anchor, while the separate stderr assertion catches it, 2 of 14. Round 1's original sabotage now fails 3 of 14, up from 2 of 5, because the new missing-006 case asserts exit status too.

THE VERIFIER ATTACKED THE NEW ASSERTION ITSELF AND FOUND ONE RESIDUAL HOLE, recorded rather than gated. A novel sentence ("Schema good to go") passes 14/14 — exactly the limit the submitter disclosed in the test comment, so no overclaim. And ANCHOR RELOCATION: planting a decoy "Verifying schema against the catalog (deferred)" at the connect stage, plus the round-1 literal via process.stdout.write, gives 14/14, because verifyAt uses indexOf and a duplicated marker moves the measurement point to the top. One-line hardening: lastIndexOf, or assert the marker appears exactly once. Not grounds to fail — it needs a planted duplicate of the marker string, unlike swapping the print call which the runner genuinely does at :190; the submission never claims anchor robustness; and the accept's own teeth survive it, since exit 1 and the INCOMPLETE line still fire.

JUDGEMENTS. The enumeration is ACCEPTABLE: it is a supplement, not the load-bearing assertion — the hard teeth are status === 1 and "an incomplete database must not print the success sentence at all", neither depending on the phrase list. It covers the whole historical failure family, generalises two into patterns, reads printed output so the print call is irrelevant, and states its own limit rather than pretending to be a detector. Semantic detection in a unit test would be worse: unfalsifiable and flaky. The UNCONDITIONAL STDERR BAN is broad but correct to keep — it is only ever evaluated against two scenarios, neither taking the catch path, and it is the only thing catching a verdict on stderr. Narrowing it by exempting "Migration failed:" would reopen a bypass.

THE CHECKSUM COMMENT NOW MATCHES THE CODE, clause by clause against :215-221: the DO UPDATE does overwrite; first_applied_at is absent from the update list so it preserves a timestamp not a checksum; priorChecksums is read once at :158-161 before the loop, so the warning does fire once and go silent. "Nothing tests the drift path" is true — grep for the warning string and priorChecksums across the test glob returns nothing. The reason for acceptance is stated along with the cost of the alternative. AND THE FALSE CLAIM WAS CORRECTED AT ITS SOURCE, not only where it was caught: migrationsLedger.test.mjs:85-90 now says it scans arguments in the source rather than what the script prints, names both prior evasions, and hands off to the real teeth.

THE VERIFIER WROTE NOTHING TO PRODUCTION AND RAN NO QUERY AGAINST IT — no psql, no setup:db, no dotenv load; the spawned runner resolved "pg" to the stub, proven by a marker only the stub emits. No credential printed, no .env file read or grepped. Suite 1034/1025/0/9 before and after, diff 125/21 across exactly the three cited files, no bare catch, no fail-soft, no ?? 0.

ONE LOOSE DESCRIPTION, not false: the commit says the ledger test "is renamed to name its four literals"; the title says "four banned literals" without enumerating them, and the literals are at :124. The title no longer overclaims, which was the actual defect.

tasks.title: Agents grep secrets into transcripts; the exclusion must be in the brief, not the discipline
tasks.detail: Two verifiers on R0.1.6 leaked credentials into their transcripts by running unscoped greps that matched .env.local — one printed most of a retired MiMo key, the other a full GSC service-account private key (R0.1.15). Both disclosed it themselves, which is the system working, but the second happened AFTER the first was reported, which is the system not learning. The rule currently lives in whatever the controller remembers to type into each prompt. It belongs in the agent definitions under .claude/agents/ so every rebuild-verifier, rebuild-implementer, rebuild-surveyor and rebuild-scribe carries it by construction: never print a credential value, and always pass --exclude='.env*' (or an equivalent path filter) to any recursive search. A repo-level guard is worth considering too — a test asserting no tracked file contains a private-key header would not catch a transcript leak, but a .gitignore check and a documented grep idiom would reduce the surface. Standing rule 9: a change to the orchestration tooling is itself ledger work.
tasks.accept: Every rebuild-* agent definition carries the never-print-a-credential rule and the --exclude='.env*' idiom; a fresh agent spawned from each definition can quote the rule back without being told it in its prompt.

tasks.title: The checksum drift warning asserts a schema mismatch that may not exist
tasks.detail: scripts/setup-supabase.mjs hashes the whole migration file after normalising line endings and trailing whitespace, but NOT comment text. So a comment-only edit changes the checksum and the runner prints 'The file no longer describes what is in the database.' R1.2.2 produced exactly this: correcting a false header comment in 010_probe_tasks.sql moved the hash from be27ae10f9467429 to ed5bc223145c0461 while the deployed SQL was verified byte-identical, 232 non-comment lines unchanged. The warning is therefore FALSE in this instance — the file describes the database exactly. Repeated comment-only drifts train an operator to wave the warning through, which is how a real drift eventually gets missed, and that would undo what R6.1.1 just closed. Two options: hash comment-stripped SQL so only semantic changes trip the warning, or keep hashing the whole file and reword the message to say the file TEXT changed rather than asserting a schema mismatch. Found by the R1.2.2 verifier.
tasks.accept: A comment-only edit to a migration either does not trip the drift warning, or trips a message that does not claim the schema differs; a test covers both a comment-only edit and a real SQL change, and fails if they report the same thing.

notes.text: filed mid-rebuild
claimed

Chose BOTH options, deliberately, because rewording alone cannot satisfy the accept (it would report the same thing for a comment edit and a SQL edit). The whole-file checksum is left byte-for-byte as it was — verified 010 still hashes to ed5bc223145c0461 through the new code — because redefining it would make the first run after this merge warn on all eleven migrations at once, which is the desensitisation the task exists to stop. A second comment-independent hash is recorded alongside it in a new nullable schema_migrations.sql_checksum column (ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, in SCHEMA_MIGRATIONS_DDL at line 48, applied before the SELECT that reads it, same commit). classifyDrift (line 335) then produces three DIFFERENT sentences (driftMessage, line 353): 'the SQL has CHANGED ... no longer describes what is in the database' for a real change; 'COMMENTS ONLY changed ... this is not a schema drift' for a comment edit; and for a row that predates the column — which is 010 in production right now — 'the file TEXT changed ... but whether the SQL changed is UNKNOWN', which claims neither. The stripper (semanticSql, line 166) is a real lexer over line comments, nestable block comments, '' and E'' strings, quoted identifiers and dollar-quoted blocks; it deliberately does NOT strip comments inside a dollar-quoted body (that body is lexically a literal, and under-stripping degrades safely to today's behaviour), and it refuses with reliable:false on anything it cannot finish reading, which routes to UNKNOWN rather than to the reassuring message. checksumsFor (line 296) also re-strips its own output as an idempotence self-check. Both accept cases are covered: comment-only edit at migrationsRunner.test.mjs:480 (real 010 text, header comment rewritten + a trailing comment added: whole-file hash moves, sql_checksum does not), real SQL change at :507, and the end-to-end message test at :614 spawns the runner with a fabricated ledger row for each of the three cases and asserts all three printed lines differ. Teeth proved by sabotage, each applied and diffed then reverted: collapsing driftMessage to one sentence fails :614; the naive /--.*/ strip the task warned about fails the dollar-quote, string-literal and unparseable tests; classifyDrift always returning 'comment' fails :614. main() now runs under an entrypoint guard (line 566) so the helpers are importable; the guard is exercised by the eight spawn tests and by  with no creds, which still exits 1 on missing credentials. No database was contacted and 010's stale production checksum was not touched. node --test migrationsRunner+migrationsLedger: 23/23.

verification.note:
VERIFIED by an independent agent, with the most thorough adversarial sweep of this rebuild so far. THEY TOOK BOTH OPTIONS AND ADDED A THIRD STATE: comment-stripped hashing AND a reworded message, keeping the original whole-file checksum as the ledger identity and recording a comment-independent hash in a new nullable sql_checksum column. classifyDrift emits three distinct sentences — sql ("the SQL has CHANGED ... no longer describes what is in the database"), comment ("COMMENTS ONLY changed ... this is not a schema drift"), and unknown ("the file TEXT changed ... whether the SQL changed is UNKNOWN ... this run cannot tell you"). Not redefining checksum is the right call: redefining it would have tripped a drift warning on EVERY migration on the first run after merge, which is the same desensitisation this task exists to stop.

THE R1.2.2 FALSE WARNING REPRODUCED END TO END on the pre-fix runner, with the ticket's numbers matching exactly: be27ae10f9467429 -> ed5bc223145c0461, printing "no longer describes what is in the database", while the new comment-independent hash 8653a0cf0838eebe is unchanged. The same fixture on the new runner yields the UNKNOWN sentence for the ACTUAL PRODUCTION ROW TODAY (sql_checksum null), the COMMENTS ONLY sentence when the semantic hash matches, and the loud SQL sentence when it does not.

THE STRIPPER WAS ATTACKED HARD AND NO COLLISION WAS FOUND. semanticSql is a four-context lexer — single quotes with '' and E-prefixed backslash escapes, double-quoted identifiers, nestable block comments, dollar-quoted blocks — plus an idempotence self-check and a reliable:false refusal that degrades to UNKNOWN, never to reassurance. Eleven hand-built adversarial pairs all reported DIFF: -- inside dollar-quoted bodies, inside single-quoted literals, '' escapes, E-strings with backslash-escaped quotes, U& strings, quoted identifiers containing --, positional params vs dollar tags, nested inner $$ inside an outer tag, unicode dollar tags, dollar-bearing identifiers, and token fusion. Then a whole-corpus sweep across all 11 migrations: 404 comment mutations left the semantic hash untouched with ZERO moving it, and 767 SQL-line mutations ALL moved it with ZERO hidden. All 11 migrations parse reliable:true.

SIX SABOTAGES, each diffed against a pristine copy outside git and node --check'd, and the accept's "fails if they report the same thing" holds in BOTH directions: a naive regex strip fails 3; reverting the fix fails 3; collapsing comment into sql fails 1; collapsing sql into comment fails 1; and the unknown verdict borrowing the reassuring comment wording fails 1.

R6.1.1 NON-REGRESSION SABOTAGE-PROVEN: INCOMPLETE with exit 0 fails 3 including the C10 case; moving the ledger INSERT after COMMIT fails the inside-the-transaction test; a verdict printed before the verify stage fails both ORDERING tests.

MIGRATION 011's EXPECTED_OBJECTS ENTRY IS CORRECT, every name and line checked against the file: table at 78, four indexes at 163/169/176/183, three functions at 220/257/299 — and all three carry kind:"function", routed to pg_proc JOIN pg_namespace rather than to_regclass, which is the check that caught 009's table-present/function-absent state.

NOTHING WAS WRITTEN AND NOTHING CONNECTED. The only new write is sql_checksum added to the existing upsert's column list; the stale 010 checksum is not patched by any new statement and still self-heals through the pre-existing ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE. The new ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS is nullable and undefaulted, so pre-existing rows read as "not known" rather than being backfilled from today's file — the lesson from the first_applied_at incident, applied.

THE NEW ENTRYPOINT GUARD WAS TRACED, NOT READ: spawned four ways including the exact npm run setup:db shape, an absolute path, a lowercased drive letter and a renamed copy. All ran main; the mismatch branch is loud with exit 1, not silent.

TWO RESIDUALS RECORDED, neither blocking. Line comments terminate on \n only, while PostgreSQL's lexer also terminates on \r, so a classic-Mac lone-CR file could collide in the reassuring direction — unreachable today (every migration has loneCR=0 and .gitattributes pins eol=lf) and a one-line fix later. And comments INSIDE dollar-quoted bodies are deliberately not stripped, costing 42 of 446 comment lines; accepted because it is the safe direction, because CREATE OR REPLACE stores the body verbatim in pg_proc.prosrc so an in-body comment edit genuinely does make the file differ from what is deployed, and because the defect instance is outside any body. Documented in-source and asserted by a test that names it as intentional.

Also recorded: a pre-existing weakness in the transaction test, which compares txn ids of the nearest enclosing BEGIN/COMMIT so an artificial split passes — untouched by this diff, and the runner source is correct. All seven evidence citations land on the mechanism they name. Suite 1106/1087/0/19. This commit also carried R6.1.6 and the 011 entry, all three disclosed in the body rather than folded in silently.

tasks.title: The ordering guard trusts the runner self-report as the stage marker
tasks.detail: R6.1.6 closed the planted-duplicate evasion by measuring from the last occurrence of the verify-stage anchor and asserting it appears exactly once. Its verifier then found two evasions that survive, and confirmed both also pass against the PRE-FIX tree, so they are pre-existing and mathematically unaffected by indexOf versus lastIndexOf. First: MOVE the sole anchor to the connect stage and have the real verify stage announce itself in different words, and the runner prints a success verdict before any migration has run, at exit 0, 23 of 23 green. Second: print the verdict after the anchor announcement but before any object is probed, also 23 of 23. The common cause is that the guard trusts a string the runner prints about itself as the marker for a stage, so relocating or straddling that marker still works. Same family as C10, different mechanism. The C10 hard teeth survive both: a DB missing 006 still exits 1 and still prints INCOMPLETE.
tasks.accept: A relocated or straddled stage marker can no longer hide a verdict printed before the catalog is actually probed. The guard keys on an event the runner cannot trivially move, such as the first per-object probe line, rather than on a self-reported banner; both evasions are covered by tests and fail if the anchoring reverts.

Six files — brightdata, perplexity, chatgpt, firecrawl, gateway-catalog, and the pre-existing mimo. All carry status headers and pass the docStatus guard. The verifier traced getSerpProvider itself: serp.js:11 SERP_PROVIDER; :12,:14 via getBrightDataApiKey to brightdata.js:7 BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY; :13,:15 via resolveSerpCredentials to serp.js:24 SERPAPI_KEY. verification.note:
VERIFIED on re-submission by a second independent verifier at 7e45990. Both clauses met.

CLAUSE 1: full suite 974 pass / 0 fail WITH the real BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY exported ambiently, and keyless, and via npm run test:scoring with the guard's diagnostic visibly printing "set (len 36)" so the run is demonstrably not vacuous. serp.test.mjs is 7/0 in all three configs — keyless, key ambient, and key with SERP_PROVIDER=brightdata forced.

CLAUSE 2 VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY OF THE FILE'S OWN GUARD, which is the right way to check a guard. The verifier wrote an out-of-band observer that snapshots the four vars, dynamically imports serp.test.mjs, and prints from process.on('exit') — after every test and every hook. All four vars come back strictly === their start values, keyed and keyless. Identity comparison on the real strings rules out a same-length substitute.

FIVE SABOTAGES, NONE OF THEM EDITING serp.test.mjs — each was a generated sibling copy outside the *.test.mjs glob, with the transform asserting non-no-op and printing the mutated region. S1 reverting the :65/:72 ordering reproduces the round-1 defect byte for byte: 6/1 with "started set (len 36), ended set (len 10)" and the observer confirming identical=false. S2 dropping BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY from SERP_ENV gives 3/4 keyed and 6/1 keyless, matching the claim exactly. S3 neutering useSerpEnv's restore catches the SERPAPI_KEY mock-key leak. S5 restoring a SAME-LENGTH fake ('X'.repeat(36)) still fails with "holding a different value" — the guard is not fooled by a fabricated credential of the right shape.

THE ORDERING MECHANISM WAS VERIFIED, NOT ASSUMED: a separate probe established that node:test runs top-level tests sequentially in registration order, runs t.after hooks in registration order, and completes all of test N's hooks before test N+1's body — so :246 observes the true post-hook state of everything above it.

THE APPEND-BELOW-:246 FRAGILITY IS REAL AND WAS DEMONSTRATED: S4 appends a leaking test below the guard and the file reports 8/0 GREEN while the observer shows SERPAPI_KEY leaking. Accepted here because it is coverage decay rather than runtime false-success — the guard cannot lie, it can only stop looking — the accept does not ask for position independence, and :247-255 warns future editors. The immune version was verified to work and costs nothing: a file-scoped after() imported from node:test, registered anywhere, runs after EVERY test in the file including appended ones, and node:test reports the thrown assertion as a file-level failure. Filed as a follow-up.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE IMPLEMENTER'S REASONING, right conclusion by the wrong mechanism: the note claims the keyless bite for the round-1 bug comes from the SERPAPI_KEY/mock-key path. Measured, it does not — under the ordering bug useSerpEnv's hook still deletes SERPAPI_KEY correctly. The true keyless bite is stronger: BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY goes unset -> 'bd-ambient', i.e. the file CONJURES A CREDENTIAL FROM NOTHING, which is the more serious shape.

LENGTH DISCLOSURE JUDGED CORRECT TO KEEP: it is load-bearing, not incidental. "started set (len 36), ended set (len 10)" is what makes the failure diagnosable; a bare "set" would render the round-1 defect as "started set, ended set", which reads like a nothing-burger. The equal-length case is already covered without disclosure by the "holding a different value" suffix, and check-secrets.mjs:268 is a real precedent whose citation resolves.

Branch-var enumeration re-confirmed as three (SERP_PROVIDER, BRIGHTDATA_API_KEY via brightdata.js:7, SERPAPI_KEY via resolveSerpCredentials) with BRIGHTDATA_SERP_ZONE a harmless superset; and no module in the import graph writes process.env at load, so PROCESS_START_ENV really is the inherited environment. That is coverage decay rather than runtime false-success — the guard cannot lie, it can only stop looking — and the R6.5.4 accept did not ask for position independence, so it was not grounds to reject. The immune form was verified to work by that same verifier and costs nothing: a file-scoped after() imported from node:test, registered anywhere, runs after EVERY test in the file including appended ones, and node:test reports the thrown assertion as a file-level failure. Same treatment is worth considering for any other file using the useSerpEnv idiom.
tasks.accept: Appending a test that leaks an env var below the guard makes the file fail; proven by adding such a test, watching it go red, and removing it.

tasks.title: gemini.js abort signal never reaches the SDK
tasks.detail: src/lib/gemini.js:46 passes { requestOptions } where the @google/generative-ai SDK expects requestOptions directly. Confirmed twice by direct SDK comparison at version 0.24.1: with the shipped shape the fetch init keys are method, headers, body and there is NO signal; with the correct nesting the keys include signal. So the AbortController is inert and Promise.race is the only timeout — the request is abandoned, not cancelled, and up to 15 in-flight requests from the five-model fallback ladder can outlive the call that started them. On the long-lived worker in R1.2 that is a socket and quota leak rather than a slow request. Found by the R6.3.1 scribe while documenting the vendor and independently reproduced by its verifier.
tasks.accept: The abort signal reaches the SDK's fetch, proven by asserting the init object carries signal; an aborted call stops the upstream request rather than merely abandoning it, and a test fails if the argument shape regresses.

gemini.js:56 now passes requestOptions DIRECTLY (was: model.generateContent(prompt, { requestOptions })). Reproduced BEFORE fixing: with the shipped shape the fetch init keys were exactly [body, headers, method] with no signal, and all 15 ladder requests were still live at return; the test file run against unfixed gemini.js failed 4/6 with exactly that evidence. After the fix the init carries a signal and the ladder failure changed from 'Gemini timeout' (abandoned) to GoogleGenerativeAIAbortError 'Request aborted when fetching ...' (cancelled). Cancellation vs abandonment proven three ways: the stub's signal fires abort exactly once per attempt, the stub fetch rejects AbortError, and the SDK surfaces the abort error. Note SDK 0.24.1 relays the caller signal through its OWN internal controller, so identity is impossible by construction; the test asserts linkage (init.signal !== ours AND aborts when ours does) and asserts init.signal !== undefined under a requestOptions that carries NO timeout, so a signal there can only have come from the call's controller. gemini.js:55 drops the SDK 'timeout' field on purpose: buildFetchOptions schedules a setTimeout(abort) it never clears, stranding one timer per rung (measured via process.getActiveResourcesInfo) - the same leak, moved. gemini.js:92-94 adds a finally that clears both deadlines and aborts the rung before the ladder advances. Regression guard at geminiAbort.test.mjs:155 asserts arg.requestOptions === undefined and arg.signal instanceof AbortSignal, captured by wrapping GoogleGenerativeAI.prototype.getGenerativeModel. Sabotage battery, 5 mutations, each proven applied: re-wrap => 4 fails; drop clearTimeout(timeoutId) => 2 fails; drop clearTimeout(raceTimeoutId) => 2 fails; re-add SDK timeout => 3 fails; drop controller.abort() from finally => 0 fails, disclosed in the code comment at gemini.js:88-91 as belt-and-braces rather than test-proven, because today the abort deadline and the race deadline fire at the same instant. No live vendor calls: globalThis.fetch stubbed in all 8 tests, GEMINI_API_KEY overwritten with a fake, no --env-file. npm run test:scoring: 1057 tests, 1047 pass, 1 fail, 9 skipped; the single failure is docStatus.test.mjs 'README migration table lists every migration on disk' over the untracked supabase/migrations/011_scan_runs.sql from a concurrent implementer, not mine. Touched only src/lib/gemini.js and the new src/lib/geminiAbort.test.mjs. Had to run claim first: the task was still todo with owner null and submit is gated on in_progress.

verification.note:
VERIFIED by an independent agent with its own harness, not the implementer's tests. REPRODUCED at the true pre-fix commit ee5504e~1 (the verifier corrected my brief): stubbing globalThis.fetch, the init keys were body/headers/method with signal UNDEFINED, and after a 20s deadline 5 of 5 ladder requests were STILL LIVE with zero abort events. At HEAD the same harness gives signal present, 0 of 5 live, and 5 abort events. With retries=2, 15 of 15 are torn down.

SIGNAL IDENTITY: the note's claim that object identity is impossible is TRUE and was verified in the SDK source rather than taken on trust — @google/generative-ai/dist/index.mjs:439-454 builds its OWN AbortController and relays via addEventListener, so the caller's signal object can never appear on the init. The tests do not settle for presence: substituting a foreign, never-aborted AbortSignal — which satisfies "an AbortSignal is present" and passes the flat-shape guard — FAILS 3 tests. Linkage is distinguished from presence.

CANCELLATION, NOT ABANDONMENT, on three independent observations: the stub's signal fires abort once per attempt; the fetch rejects with an AbortError so the chain terminates; and the SDK surfaces GoogleGenerativeAIAbortError instead of the old "Gemini timeout", which is exactly the change of error identity that distinguishes the two. The residual limit is honest and unavoidable — real socket teardown is undici's behaviour on init.signal and no stub can prove it; the mechanism reaching undici is proven correct.

A SECOND LEAK WAS FOUND AND CLOSED BY THE IMPLEMENTER ON THEIR OWN: clearTimeout ran only on the success path and the race timer was never cleared at all. The finally block clears both, measured via process.getActiveResourcesInfo as 0 pending Timeout resources after a 5-rung failure. Dropping the SDK's own timeout field is justified rather than a shortcut — the SDK schedules setTimeout(abort) and NEVER clears it, which would strand one timer per rung, relocating the leak.

SIX SABOTAGES, each diff-proven applied: the shipped { requestOptions } shape fails 4; a full revert fails 6 of 8; the foreign signal fails 3; re-adding the SDK timeout fails 3; dropping clearTimeout fails 2; dropping controller.abort() from finally fails 0 — the implementer's own disclosure, and accurate: the abort deadline timer is registered before the race timer with the same delay so Node fires abort first, making that line belt-and-braces today. It is disclosed in the code rather than dressed up as test-proven, which is the honest handling.

SDK VERSION: 0.24.1 installed, declared as a caret range and not pinned, though the lockfile resolves deterministically for npm ci. The implementer gets credit they did not claim — geminiAbort.test.mjs:97 and :124 pin the SDK's OWN behaviour, asserting the wrapper shape yields no signal and the flat shape does, so a version bump that flipped the argument shape fails loudly rather than silently reinstating an inert controller. The assumption is executable, not documentary.

LIVENESS rebuilt: POST /api/opportunities is served by Next regardless of in-repo callers and sits behind the operator perimeter, so it is reachable by any authenticated operator client; its only shipped browser caller has zero importers, and the other three importers of gemini.js are dead. The leak was real but currently unexercised. Suite 1106/1087/0/19, no live vendor call, main repo never written to.

TWO STALE FIGURES IN THE NOTE, neither a false claim about the shipped code: "failed 4/6" matches no configuration at HEAD (a full revert fails 6 of 8, the isolated re-wrap 4 of 8; the figure describes an intermediate draft), and the quoted suite count predates the 011 commit.

FOLLOW-UP FILED, and it is a direct consequence of this fix landing: docs/vendors/gemini.md now asserts a fixed bug as current — its quirk 3 heading says the SDK never receives the signal, its contract row says the timeout is enforced by Promise.race only, and every citation in that section now resolves to unrelated code. No test guards vendor-doc citations, so the suite will not catch it. The implementer was right not to widen the diff into a governed doc.
